prompt.context: A health insurance company experienced a loss of $40M this year, after recording a $40M profit last year. They have hired us to determine the cause(s) of this decline and identify potential solutions. The company is in only one line of business, Commercial Risk Insurance, in only one region. They have several direct competitors. Their cash flows originate from premiums, which are paid in on a periodic basis by its customers, and claims are paid out to the customers' caregivers as appropriate. For the sake of simplicity, the company's Profit = Premiums – Claims. Currently this company has 4 million members, which equates to a 40% market share. All revenue, cost and profit figures are measured on a per-member basis.
prompt.question: How would you go about identifying potential solutions for their decline in profitability?

clarifying_info.q: Have premiums charged per member changed over the last year?
clarifying_info.a: No, they have been stable at an average of $200/year/member.
The member base has been stable at 4 million members, so revenues have been stable as well.

clarifying_info.q: Have they made any large capital investments recently?
clarifying_info.a: No large capital expenditures except for a new claims payment system two years ago. In general, this is not a capital-intensive business.

clarifying_info.q: Have per-member variable costs been changing?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, per-member variable costs are rising by $20/member/year.

clarifying_info.q: What is driving the increase in variable costs?
clarifying_info.a: The biggest cost driver is utilization — how frequently doctors use other sources for a patient's care.

clarifying_info.q: How is the company organized internally?
clarifying_info.a: There are several functional groups: New Admits, Pre-authorizations, and Case Management. These groups are staffed with MDs and RNs that used to be in the field treating patients. They are now responsible for managing hundreds of doctors and nurses currently treating patients.

clarifying_info.q: Are the MDs and RNs managing those groups experienced with managing large organizations?
clarifying_info.a: No, they are more accustomed to working in practices of 5–10 professionals and are unaccustomed to managing such large staff.

clarifying_info.q: What is the background of upper management?
clarifying_info.a: Upper management are also MDs that used to be in the field.

framework: Diagnose profitability using Profit = Revenue – Costs
Revenue = Price × Quantity (Premiums per member × Number of members)
Costs = Fixed costs + Variable costs (Claims/utilization costs)
Isolate which side has changed: stable revenue → focus on costs
Within costs, identify the driver: utilization rising due to poor management
Explore internal organizational factors: structure, skills, systems, staffing, leadership
Identify solutions to address root cause (management capability gap)

questions.prompt: Calculate total variable costs last year and this year, then derive per-member variable costs for each year.
questions.guidance: Use the profit equation and known figures to back into total costs, then divide by membership.

math.answer: Variable costs rose from $190/member/year to $210/member/year, an increase of $20/member/year, totaling an $80M swing in profit ($40M profit to –$40M loss).

questions.prompt: What factors might be driving the increase in utilization (i.e., how frequently doctors use outside resources for patient care)?
questions.guidance: A strong answer covers both external and internal drivers. External: rising malpractice risk causing more second opinions, changing physician prescribing habits, cost of care (drugs, equipment). Internal: quality of management of field MDs/RNs, information systems available to case managers, organizational structure and oversight processes.

questions.prompt: Looking inside the company, where would you look to diagnose the management problem causing the utilization increase?
questions.guidance: Apply an organizational diagnostics lens (e.g., McKinsey 7-S or similar): Strategy, Skills of clinical managers, Shared values, Staffing, Systems/technology, Leadership, and organizational Structure. Key insight: MDs and RNs in internal functional groups (New Admits, Pre-authorizations, Case Management) were trained as clinicians in small practices of 5–10 people, not as managers of large remote teams, leading to poor control over referrals and unnecessary testing/procedures.

brainstorming.prompt: What are potential solutions to address the management capability gap causing rising utilization costs?

categories.name: Information Systems
ideas: Consolidate data view for each functional group so case managers have all necessary information
Implement a unified dashboard for New Admits, Pre-authorizations, and Case Management
Upgrade the claims payment system to include real-time utilization tracking

categories.name: Training and Development
ideas: Provide leadership and management training for clinical staff now in managerial roles
Develop change-management programs to transition MDs/RNs from small-practice mindset to large-org management
Bring in professional managers to partner with or coach clinical leaders

categories.name: Organizational Structure
ideas: Hire professional healthcare administrators to manage large teams, with MDs in advisory/clinical oversight roles
Restructure reporting lines to reduce span of control to manageable levels
Create clear protocols and guidelines for referrals and pre-authorizations to reduce discretionary utilization

categories.name: Incentive Design
ideas: Tie physician and case manager compensation partly to utilization efficiency metrics
Set benchmarks for referral rates and unnecessary procedures by specialty

categories.name: Process and Controls
ideas: Implement peer-review processes for high-cost referrals and procedures
Introduce utilization review protocols with clear thresholds requiring escalation

recommendation: The primary cause of the $80M profit decline is a $20/member/year rise in variable (utilization) costs, while revenues remained flat at $800M

The root cause is a management capability gap: internal clinical staff in New Admits, Pre-authorizations, and Case Management groups lack the experience to manage large remote teams, leading to uncontrolled referrals and unnecessary procedures
risks: Solutions involving management restructuring may face resistance from clinical staff accustomed to autonomy
Training programs take time to yield results; utilization costs may continue to rise in the near term
Hiring professional managers could create cultural friction with MD/RN workforce
next_steps: Audit current information systems across the three functional groups and define consolidated data requirements
Design and roll out a leadership and management training program for clinical managers
Review organizational structure and span of control; consider pairing clinical managers with experienced healthcare administrators
Establish utilization benchmarks and a monitoring dashboard to track improvement over time
